source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (JAMA Netw Open 7:e2440969)
finding: Giving physicians GPT-4 (ChatGPT Plus) did not raise their diagnostic reasoning score over UpToDate/Google.
numbers: 50 US physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), 25 per arm, 244 cases. Median score 76% (IQR 66-87) LLM arm vs 74% (63-84) control. Adjusted diff 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, P=.60). Power was set to detect 8 points.
quote: The availability of an LLM to physicians as a diagnostic aid did not significantly improve clinical reasoning compared with conventional resources
limits: Six vignettes, 60 minutes, one commercial model, no prompt training. Small sample; CI cannot rule out a modest gain or loss.
agent_relevance: Access to a strong model is not the same as using it well. A scaffold must control how the model is used, not just offer it.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (JAMA Netw Open 7:e2440969)
finding: The LLM alone beat both physician groups. Humans plus LLM did worse than LLM alone.
numbers: LLM alone: 3 runs, median 92% (IQR 82-97). Versus conventional-resource physicians: +16 points (95% CI 2-30, P=.03). Versus physicians with LLM: about 16 points higher (76% vs 92%, descriptive).
limits: Only 6 cases, 3 LLM runs, prompt iteratively developed by authors. The cases were never released, so training contamination is unlikely.
agent_relevance: The human-in-the-loop step lost most of the model's skill. In our single agent the program should carry the model's output forward, not rely on a person to re-read it.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (JAMA Netw Open 7:e2440969)
finding: Secondary outcomes: time and final-diagnosis accuracy showed no clear gain.
numbers: Time per case 519 s (IQR 371-668) LLM vs 565 s (456-788); diff -82 s (95% CI -195 to 31, P=.20). Final diagnosis odds ratio 1.4 ordinal (95% CI 0.7-2.8) and 1.9 binary (0.9-4.0, P=.10).
limits: Not corrected for multiple comparisons. Wide intervals.
agent_relevance: Speed gains are not shown; do not count on time savings as evidence.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (JAMA Netw Open 7:e2440969)
finding: All 22 of 22 readable transcripts in the LLM arm show physicians used the LLM, yet no gain. Subgroups (attending vs resident, heavy vs light prior LLM use) looked the same.
numbers: Attending diff 0.5 points (P=.92); resident 3 points (P=.50); LLM use more than monthly 5 points (95% CI -7 to 16, P=.40); less than monthly -0.5 points. 3 transcripts lost.
limits: Subgroups underpowered. Physicians used the chat freely, with no set protocol.
agent_relevance: Non-use is not the explanation. The interaction pattern is the weak point, which supports a fixed protocol (G-rules) over free chat.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (JAMA Netw Open 7:e2440969)
finding: Method: the outcome was a structured-reflection rubric, not just final-diagnosis accuracy. It scored differential accuracy, supporting and opposing factors, and next steps.
numbers: Graders weighted kappa 0.66 across 3 graders; Cronbach alpha 0.64 (0.67 without final diagnosis). Cases adapted from the landmark Bond-style set, 105 available, 6 chosen by nominal group technique.
limits: Moderate reliability. Rubric rewards thorough written reasoning, which favours a model that writes a lot.
agent_relevance: A rubric for opposing evidence and next test could be a cheap check of our O-operators on a clinical task.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models (arXiv 2312.00164; later Nature 2025)
finding: A PaLM 2 model tuned for diagnosis beat unassisted clinicians on 302 NEJM case reports when used alone.
numbers: 302 NEJM CPC cases. LLM alone: top-1 29.2%, top-10 59.1%. Unassisted clinicians: top-1 15.9%, top-10 33.6% (p=0.04).
limits: NEJM CPC cases are very hard and text only. 20 clinicians, each case read by two. Some cases may overlap with training data; 56 non-overlap cases gave top-1 35.4%, top-10 55.4%.
agent_relevance: LLM standalone differentials can be strong. Top-10 list recall is a useful target for a differential-generating operator.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
finding: LLM assistance helped clinicians more than search did in this study (unlike Goh 2024).
numbers: Top-10 accuracy: LLM-assisted 51.8% (table) vs search-assisted 44.5% vs unassisted 33.6-36.1%. Abstract: 51.7% vs 36.1% unassisted (McNemar 45.7, p<0.01) and 44.4% with search (p=0.03). Top-1: 25.2% LLM-assisted vs 24.3% search-assisted.
limits: Clinicians gave an unassisted list first, then re-did it with the tool (a two-step design). Top-1 gain is tiny. Clinicians asked the LLM about 2.9 questions on average. Outcome is list inclusion, not reasoning quality.
agent_relevance: Difference from Goh: here the clinician already had a list and the LLM extended it. An add-candidates step after the first attempt may help, as O-operators suggest.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
finding: Method detail: model-based scoring and Bond-style quality score were used alongside human raters. Clinicians were told not to ask for data not in the case.
numbers: 19 to 20 board-certified clinicians (median 14 years); two lists per case from each condition plus the standalone LLM list. Date check: 51 of 302 cases (16.9%) were from the recent period used for the overlap analysis.
limits: Cases published in a journal; contamination risk cannot be excluded.
agent_relevance: Use held-out and recent cases when we test on clinical vignettes.

source: Kanjee, Crowe, Rodman (2023) Accuracy of a generative AI model in a complex diagnostic challenge (JAMA 330:78)
finding: First JAMA test of GPT-4 on NEJM CPCs: top diagnosis right in 39%, correct diagnosis in differential in 64%.
numbers: 70 of 80 cases (2021-2022; 10 excluded). Top-1 27/70 = 39%. In differential 45/70 = 64%. Mean differential length 9.0 (SD 1.4). Mean rank of correct item 2.5 (SD 2.5). Quality score mean 4.2 (SD 1.3), median 5.
limits: Scorers agreed on 66% (kappa 0.57). Single prompt developed on 7 cases. Training data ended Sept 2021, so some cases may be contaminated. No human comparison.
agent_relevance: Baseline for GPT-4 era: roughly 40% top-1, 64% top-N on hard CPCs. Later models (o1-preview) went far higher.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (arXiv 2412.10849)
finding: o1-preview on NEJM CPCs: correct diagnosis in differential 78.3%, first diagnosis correct 52%.
numbers: 143 CPCs. In differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7-84.8); top-1 52% (44-61). Before vs after training cutoff 79.8% vs 73.5% (p=0.59). On 70 cases from the GPT-4 study: exact or very close 88.6% vs GPT-4 72.9%.
limits: Preprint. Historical GPT-4 control from a different setting and prompt. CPCs are published, so contamination possible; the cutoff split did not show a drop.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained models beat GPT-4 by about 12-16 points on the same cases. Stronger base reasoning matters more than the prompt.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview picked the right next test in 87.5% of CPC cases; a perfect R-IDEA reasoning score in 78 of 80 NEJM Healer cases.
numbers: Test choice: correct 87.5%, helpful 11%, unhelpful 1.5% (132 cases). R-IDEA perfect: o1 78/80, GPT-4 47/80, attendings 28/80 (all p<0.0001).
limits: Test-choice grading agreement kappa 0.28 only. R-IDEA scores written reasoning, which favours fluent models.
agent_relevance: Written-reasoning quality is easy for LLMs. Do not treat fluent rationale as proof of correct decisions (G2).

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: Management cases: o1-preview 86% vs GPT-4 42%, physicians+GPT-4 41%, physicians with conventional resources 34%. Landmark Goh cases: o1 97% vs GPT-4 92%, physicians+GPT-4 76%, physicians 74%.
numbers: Management, 5 cases: o1 minus GPT-4 +41.6 points (95% CI 22.9-60.4), minus physicians+GPT-4 +42.5, minus physicians +49.0. Landmark, 6 cases: o1 vs GPT-4 +4.4 (CI -19 to 27.7, P=0.7); vs physicians +20.2 (CI -0.4 to 40.9, P=0.055).
limits: Historical controls, different cohorts. Landmark cases are the same 6 as Goh 2024, so the 97% is near the ceiling.
agent_relevance: The Goh 2024 cases are now saturated by the model alone. Newer, harder or interactive tests are needed.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: Real emergency room cases (79): o1 beat two attendings at each of three touchpoints, with the largest edge when little information was available.
numbers: Exact or very close diagnosis (Bond 4-5): o1 65.8% at triage, 69.6% at ER physician, 79.7% at ICU admission. Physician 1: 54.4, 60.8, 75.9. Physician 2: 48.1, 50.6, 68.4. Raters could not tell AI from human: 83.5-84.6% 'cannot tell'.
limits: Only 2 physicians as baseline. Single centre. Text only.
agent_relevance: Early-stage (low information) differentials are where a model adds most. This is the S-state where candidate generation matters.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model
finding: Probabilistic reasoning: o1-preview was about the same as GPT-4 at estimating pre-test and post-test probabilities.
numbers: 5 primary-care cases; reference human sample 553 practitioners (290 residents, 202 attendings, 61 NPs/PAs). Only the coronary stress test case moved closer to the scientific reference.
limits: Probability estimation did not improve with the new model. Calibration problem remains.
agent_relevance: Do not trust model-stated probabilities; compute them with code where possible (counted, not judged steps).

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models (arXiv 2506.22405; MAI-DxO and SDBench)
finding: Scaffold result: a five-role orchestrator on o3 reached 80% accuracy (81.9% without a budget) on 304 NEJM CPC cases that unfold step by step. Physicians scored about 20%.
numbers: 304 cases; 21 US/UK generalists did 764 diagnoses on 56 test cases: 19.9% accuracy, 11.8 min, 6.6 questions, 7.2 tests, mean cost $2,963. Off-the-shelf o3: 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO (no budget): 81.9% at $4,735. Budget mode 79.9% at $2,396. Ensemble 85.5% at $7,184.
limits: Physicians could not use search, books or colleagues, which the authors say understates them. Gatekeeper is an o4-mini model with synthetic findings. Costs are estimates. Cases are published CPCs.
agent_relevance: Closest match to our design: roles Hypothesis (Bayesian ranked top-3), Test-Chooser (max discrimination, up to 3 tests), Challenger (devil's advocate), Stewardship (cost). The scaffold lifted accuracy and cut cost versus the bare model.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models (arXiv 2506.22405; MAI-DxO and SDBench)
finding: The orchestrator helps across model families and helps weaker models most. A single model plays five personas; it is not five models.
numbers: Gains significant (one-sided paired permutation test, 10000 resamples, p<0.005) for all models tested except o3 and o4-mini, which instead had significant cost cuts. Families: OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Llama. Weak models without it considered fewer diagnoses and never ordered the confirming tests ('false economy').
limits: Developed mainly with GPT-4.1 on a train split; held-out 56 cases used for the headline. Personas from one model share errors (our G4 warning).
agent_relevance: Supports a scaffold on a fixed model. The authors' reading that the Challenger cut anchoring is based on case review, not an ablation, so it is [S].

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models (arXiv 2506.22405; MAI-DxO and SDBench)
finding: Case review: bare o3 anchored on the first impression and ordered 'reasonable' tests; the orchestrator sought disconfirming evidence and asked the patient first.
numbers: Example: hand-sanitiser ingestion case. Bare o3 cost $3,431 and was wrong; MAI-DxO asked the direct question and was right at $795. Inference cost about $0.15 per case, small next to test cost.
limits: Anecdotal single case; selected by authors.
agent_relevance: Cheap questions before expensive tests is an operator we could add for tool-using tasks. Doubt here is triggered by an explicit Challenger role, not a schedule, so check against G1.

source: Tu et al. (2024) Towards conversational diagnostic AI (AMIE) (arXiv 2401.05654)
finding: AMIE, a model tuned by self-play for diagnostic dialogue, beat 20 primary care physicians in text OSCE consults on diagnosis and most rating axes.
numbers: 149 scenarios (India 75, Canada 60, UK remainder), 20 PCPs, patient actors. AMIE better on 28 of 32 specialist axes and 24 of 26 patient-actor axes. Top-k DDx accuracy higher for AMIE under bootstrap with FDR correction (exact top-k values are in figure form).
limits: Text chat is unfamiliar to PCPs and not real practice. Scripted patient actors. Authors warn not to translate directly.
agent_relevance: Information gathering plateaued within about 10 turns for both AMIE and PCPs: diagnosis quality was set early. Another sign that early candidate generation matters.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making (Nat Med 30:2613)
finding: Counter-evidence: open Llama-2-family models were worse than doctors on 2,400 real MIMIC-IV abdominal pain cases and broke guidelines.
numbers: 2,400 cases, 4 diseases (appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, pancreatitis). With full information: 80-case subset, 4 clinicians, LLMs over 20 seeds; LLMs significantly worse (P<0.001), gap 16-25 points; German residents 87.5%, senior US hospitalist 92.5%. Autonomous mode (LLM gathers data) lower still.
limits: Tested only open 70B Llama-2 models (no GPT-4 allowed on MIMIC data). Models are weak by 2026 standards. Only 4 clinicians.
agent_relevance: Note the contrast: weak open models fail, strong models succeed. Do not generalise either way; report the model with the result.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of LLMs in clinical decision-making
finding: Models were hasty, poor at lab reading, and got worse with more information.
numbers: Lab classification (low results correct): Chat 26.5%, OASST 70.2%, WizardLM 45.8%; high results: 50.1%, 77.2%, 24.1%. Physical exam asked first: Chat 97.1%, OASST 79.8%, WizardLM 53.1%. Pancreatitis accuracy for OASST 44.1%. Giving only one exam gave gains of 8.6 to 21.6 points (e.g. pancreatitis +21.6 Chat with labs only).
limits: Open 70B models; findings may not hold for frontier models. Mitigation (summarising, abnormal-only labs) tested only on these.
agent_relevance: Supports code-side checks (G2/G3): let code flag abnormal labs and present only relevant evidence. Also order effects: shuffle or fix order and check.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of LLMs in clinical decision-making
finding: Instruction and order sensitivity: accuracy shifted when only wording ('final diagnosis' vs 'reason for abdominal pain') or the order of identical information changed.
numbers: Models hallucinated nonexistent tools and needed manual correction. Order effect was disease-dependent (Fig. 6).
limits: Quantified in figures; I read the text summary, not the figure values.
agent_relevance: Matches our worry that sampling is not independent and that format matters. Add a paraphrase-check before trusting a diagnosis.

source: Goh et al. (2025) GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks: a randomized controlled trial (Nat Med)
finding: Follow-up on management reasoning: GPT-4 did help physicians. This is the success that Goh 2024 lacked.
numbers: 92 physicians (46/46), 5 vignettes, 375 scored cases. Mean total 43.0% LLM-assisted vs 35.7% conventional; diff 6.5 points (95% CI 2.7-10.2, P<0.001). LLM alone 43.7%, same as physicians+LLM (diff -0.9, 95% CI -9.0 to 7.2) and trend above conventional (+7.3, CI -0.7 to 15.4, P=0.074).
limits: Open-ended management tasks, not diagnosis. LLM users spent more time: 801.5 s vs 690.2 s (diff 119.3 s, 95% CI 17.4-221.2, P=0.02). Simulated vignettes. Only 24% frequent LLM users.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: gains appear on management (trade-offs, scripts) but not on a diagnosis task where the humans were already near the model's level. The tool's help depends on task and rubric.

source: Goh et al. (2025) GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks
finding: Subscores: the diagnostic and specific-management domains moved; factual and general did not.
numbers: Diagnostic subscore 56.8 vs 45.8 (diff 12.1, 95% CI 3.1-21.0, P=0.009). Management 40.5 vs 33.4 (6.1, P=0.001). Specific 42.4 vs 34.9 (6.2, P=0.002). Factual diff 9.6 (CI -3.1 to 22.3, P=0.14). General diff 3.3 (P=0.2). Rater kappa pooled 0.80; 82% full agreement on 400 cases.
limits: Subscore denominators are smaller (about 70 cases per arm for factual/diagnostic). Not corrected for multiple tests.
agent_relevance: Helps with case-specific reasoning, less with generic or factual items.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine (npj Digit Med 7:20)
finding: Prompting a model to imitate named clinical reasoning styles did not beat plain chain of thought for GPT-4. It hurt GPT-3.5.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on free-response MedQA: CoT 46%, intuitive 48% (+1.7, P=0.4), analytic 40% (-6, P=0.001), differential-diagnosis 38% (-8.9, P<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4.4, P=0.02). GPT-4 (498 items): CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, analytic 78%, differential 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4, P=0.07). NEJM challenge set GPT-4: CoT 38% vs differential 34% (-4.2, P=0.09).
limits: MedQA items are exam questions, not open cases. Gains were limited to interpretability, not accuracy. Small sets.
agent_relevance: Naming a clinical method (differential, Bayes) as a prompt is not a free win. This fits our rule against forced doubt (G1) and against adding a Bayesian step without a check.

source: Rao et al. (2023) Assessing the utility of ChatGPT throughout the entire clinical workflow (J Med Internet Res 25:e48659)
finding: ChatGPT did better as information accumulated: weakest at the initial differential, best at final diagnosis.
numbers: 36 Merck Manual vignettes. Overall 71.7% (95% CI 69.3-74.1). Final diagnosis 76.9% (67.8-86.1). Initial differential 60.3% (54.2-66.6). Differential diagnosis questions beta -15.8% (P<.001) and management -7.4% (P=.02) vs general knowledge.
limits: Textbook vignettes, likely in training data. Human scorers; single model; no physician baseline.
agent_relevance: Early-stage differential generation is the hard part for models, as it is for people (see Brodeur ER cases).

source: Bond et al. (2012) Differential diagnosis generators: an evaluation of currently available computer programs (J Gen Intern Med 27:213)
finding: Pre-LLM baseline for the same task: rule-based DDx generators on 20 NEJM and MKSAP cases, scored 1-5 with 5 as the exact diagnosis. This is the Bond score used in later LLM studies.
numbers: 23 programs found, 4 met criteria. Mean score: Isabel 3.45 (2.53-4.37), DxPlain 3.45 (2.63-4.27), DiagnosisPro 2.65 (1.75-3.55), PEPID 1.70 (0.71-2.69).
limits: Only 20 cases, wide intervals. Old tools used structured input, not free text.
agent_relevance: LLMs (Kanjee mean 4.2 on a similar scale, harder cases) now exceed these tools; the scale gives continuity to older work.

source: Miller, Pople, Myers (1982) INTERNIST-1; Berner et al. (1994) Performance of four computer-based diagnostic systems (NEJM)
finding: Historical line: expert-system DDx programs (INTERNIST-1/QMR, DXplain, Iliad, Meditel) were tested on hard cases from the 1980s on. Details not opened this session.
numbers: Not opened; no figures recorded.
limits: Not verified.
agent_relevance: Use as the historical frame only; cite after opening.

source: Eriksen, Moller, Ryg (2023) Use of GPT-4 to diagnose complex clinical cases (NEJM AI)
finding: Another early GPT-4 test on published hard cases, compared with readers of the journal. Not opened.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Page not read.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a replication check against Kanjee 2023 once opened.
